claim: The core CoREST complex (LHC) contains histone deacetylase HDAC1 and histone demethylase LSD1 held together by the scaffold protein CoREST.
source: The core CoREST complex (LHC) contains histone deacetylase HDAC1 and histone demethylase LSD1 held together by the scaffold protein CoREST.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about the CoREST complex composition.

claim: LHC demethylase activity toward methyl-Lys4 in histone H3 is strongly inhibited by H3 Lys14 acetylation.
source: LHC demethylase activity toward methyl-Lys4 in histone H3 is strongly inhibited by H3 Lys14 acetylation, and this appears to be an intrinsic property of the LSD1 subunit.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3 showing reduced demethylation rates with K14ac substrates.

claim: The inhibition of LHC demethylase activity by H3 Lys14 acetylation is an intrinsic property of the LSD1 subunit.
source: LHC demethylase activity toward methyl-Lys4 in histone H3 is strongly inhibited by H3 Lys14 acetylation, and this appears to be an intrinsic property of the LSD1 subunit.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing GST-LSD1 alone exhibits similar inhibition by K14ac.

claim: The deacetylase selectivity of LHC shows a marked preference for H3 acetyl-Lys9 versus acetyl-Lys14 in nucleosome substrates.
source: Moreover, the deacetylase selectivity of LHC unexpectedly shows a marked preference for H3 acetyl-Lys9 versus acetyl-Lys14 in nucleosome substrates but this selectivity is lost with isolated acetyl-Lys H3 protein.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 6 and Table 1 showing differential deacetylation rates.

claim: The deacetylase selectivity of LHC for H3 acetyl-Lys9 versus acetyl-Lys14 is lost with isolated acetyl-Lys H3 protein.
source: Moreover, the deacetylase selectivity of LHC unexpectedly shows a marked preference for H3 acetyl-Lys9 versus acetyl-Lys14 in nucleosome substrates but this selectivity is lost with isolated acetyl-Lys H3 protein.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6C and Table 1 showing similar deacetylation rates for K9ac and K14ac in isolated H3 protein.

claim: The diminished activity of LHC to Lys-14 deacetylation in nucleosomes is not merely due to steric accessibility.
source: This diminished activity of LHC to Lys-14 deacetylation in nucleosomes is not merely due to steric accessibility based on the pattern of sensitivity of the LHC enzymatic complex to hydroxamic acid-mediated inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7 showing similar Ki values for H3K9Hd and H3K14Hd nucleosomes.

claim: HDAC1 is a Class I HDAC Zn hydrolase.
source: HDAC1 is a Class I HDAC Zn hydrolase and has a broad range of targeted acetyl-lysine (Kac) sites in histones and non-histone proteins (Cole, 2008; Falkenberg and Johnstone, 2014; Taunton et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HDAC1 has a broad range of targeted acetyl-lysine (Kac) sites in histones and non-histone proteins.
source: HDAC1 is a Class I HDAC Zn hydrolase and has a broad range of targeted acetyl-lysine (Kac) sites in histones and non-histone proteins (Cole, 2008; Falkenberg and Johnstone, 2014; Taunton et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HDAC1 and HDAC2 are typically found in multi-protein repressor complexes in the cell including the CoREST complex, the NuRD complex, the MiDAC complex and the Sin3a complex.
source: HDAC1 and its closest paralog HDAC2 (sometimes the pair are called HDAC1/2) are typically found in multi-protein repressor complexes in the cell including the CoREST complex, the NuRD complex, the MiDAC complex and the Sin3a complex (Bantscheff et al., 2011; Itoh et al., 2015; Laugesen and Helin, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The CoREST complex contains HDAC1/2, LSD1, and the CoREST scaffold protein as core subunits in a 1:1:1 stoichiometry.
source: The CoREST complex which is investigated here is special because it contains HDAC1/2, LSD1, and the CoREST scaffold protein as core subunits in a 1:1:1 stoichiometry (Kalin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 2A.

claim: LSD1 is a flavin-dependent amine oxidase that demethylates mono- or di-methylated Lys4 in histone H3 (H3K4me1/2).
source: LSD1 is a flavin-dependent amine oxidase that demethylates mono- or di-methylated Lys4 in histone H3 (H3K4me1/2) (Shi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Histone Kac and methyl H3K4 modifications are typically found in regions of transcriptionally active chromatin.
source: Because histone Kac and methyl H3K4 modifications are typically found in regions of transcriptionally active chromatin, the enzymatic activities of HDAC1 and LSD1 in the CoREST complex tend to synergistically result in gene silencing (Kalin et al., 2018; Ooi and Wood, 2007) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The enzymatic activities of HDAC1 and LSD1 in the CoREST complex tend to synergistically result in gene silencing.
source: Because histone Kac and methyl H3K4 modifications are typically found in regions of transcriptionally active chromatin, the enzymatic activities of HDAC1 and LSD1 in the CoREST complex tend to synergistically result in gene silencing (Kalin et al., 2018; Ooi and Wood, 2007) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: LHC demethylase activity with unacetylated H3K4me2 tail peptide exhibits bi-phasic kinetics.
source: Interestingly, using the unacetylated H3K4me2 tail peptide, we observed a bi-phasic demethylase activity with LHC that was not observed with purified GST-LSD1 as the catalyst (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GST-LSD1 does not exhibit bi-phasic demethylase activity with unacetylated H3K4me2 tail peptide.
source: Interestingly, using the unacetylated H3K4me2 tail peptide, we observed a bi-phasic demethylase activity with LHC that was not observed with purified GST-LSD1 as the catalyst (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The first phase of LHC-catalyzed demethylation is typically about 3–5 min in duration.
source: The first phase is typically about 3–5 min in duration and after transition to the second phase, product formation is quite linear for at least 15 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After transition to the second phase, product formation in LHC-catalyzed demethylation is quite linear for at least 15 min.
source: The first phase is typically about 3–5 min in duration and after transition to the second phase, product formation is quite linear for at least 15 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The initial phase of the LHC-catalyzed reaction had lower apparent Km and kcat values compared to the second linear phase.
source: By varying the peptide substrate concentration, we determined that the initial phase of the LHC-catalyzed reaction had lower apparent Km and kcat values compared to the second linear phase and that the Km value of the second phase was similar to that of GST-LSD1 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Km value of the second phase of LHC-catalyzed demethylation was similar to that of GST-LSD1.
source: By varying the peptide substrate concentration, we determined that the initial phase of the LHC-catalyzed reaction had lower apparent Km and kcat values compared to the second linear phase and that the Km value of the second phase was similar to that of GST-LSD1 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: InsP6 somewhat prolonged the initial phase of LHC-catalyzed demethylation.
source: InsP6 somewhat prolonged the initial phase (Figure 2B) but altering the buffer conditions did not eliminate the bi-phasic nature of the reaction.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Altering the buffer conditions did not eliminate the bi-phasic nature of LHC-catalyzed demethylation.
source: InsP6 somewhat prolonged the initial phase (Figure 2B) but altering the buffer conditions did not eliminate the bi-phasic nature of the reaction.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Size exclusion chromatography of the LHC reaction mixture after 20 min showed that the complex was still intact.
source: We considered the possibility that the LHC complex might be falling apart over the course of our assays, but size exclusion chromatography of the reaction mixture after 20 min showed that the complex was still intact (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The addition of 146 bp of dsDNA sharply accelerated LHC-mediated demethylation of the H3K4me2 tail peptide in a concentration-dependent way.
source: Interestingly, we found that the addition of 146 bp of dsDNA (the 601 Widom sequence [Lowary and Widom, 1998]) sharply accelerated LHC-mediated demethylation of the H3K4me2 tail peptide in a concentration- dependent way and also abolished the lag phase seen without DNA. (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: The addition of 146 bp of dsDNA abolished the lag phase of LHC-mediated demethylation seen without DNA.
source: Interestingly, we found that the addition of 146 bp of dsDNA (the 601 Widom sequence [Lowary and Widom, 1998]) sharply accelerated LHC-mediated demethylation of the H3K4me2 tail peptide in a concentration- dependent way and also abolished the lag phase seen without DNA. (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: The dose-response curve for DNA activation of LHC showed an EC50 of 63 ± 15 ng/μL.
source: The dose-response curve showed an EC50 of 63 ± 15 ng/μL and a maximum activation of demethylation rate of 36-fold (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on dose-response analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: DNA activation of LHC showed a maximum activation of demethylation rate of 36-fold.
source: The dose-response curve showed an EC50 of 63 ± 15 ng/μL and a maximum activation of demethylation rate of 36-fold (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on dose-response analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A 4.9 kb circular DNA plasmid exhibited a similar level of stimulation of LHC catalyzed demethylation as 146 bp DNA.
source: We also tested a 4.9 kb circular DNA plasmid and a 60 bp linear dsDNA fragment. The plasmid DNA exhibited a similar level of stimulation of LHC catalyzed demethylation but the 60 bp dsDNA fragment was inert in these assay conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A 60 bp linear dsDNA fragment was inert in stimulating LHC catalyzed demethylation.
source: We also tested a 4.9 kb circular DNA plasmid and a 60 bp linear dsDNA fragment. The plasmid DNA exhibited a similar level of stimulation of LHC catalyzed demethylation but the 60 bp dsDNA fragment was inert in these assay conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A large piece of DNA appears necessary for allosteric activation of LHC-mediated demethylation of H3K4me2 tail peptide.
source: These results suggest that a large piece of DNA appears necessary for allosteric activation of LHC-mediated demethylation of H3K4me2 tail peptide, perhaps in part through a templating role.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of DNA of different lengths.

claim: When a stoichiometric level of BHC80 (or higher) relative to the LHC concentration is added, the bi-phasic demethylase activity simplified with the second phase being markedly inhibited.
source: Interestingly, when a stoichiometric level of BHC80 (or higher) relative to the LHC concentration is added, the bi-phasic demethylase activity simplified with the second phase being markedly inhibited (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The BHC80 inhibitory effect appeared to saturate at 200 nM.
source: The BHC80 inhibitory effect appeared to saturate at 200 nM and it had only a slight impact on the initial phase of the demethylation reaction (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: BHC80 had only a slight impact on the initial phase of the LHC demethylation reaction.
source: The BHC80 inhibitory effect appeared to saturate at 200 nM and it had only a slight impact on the initial phase of the demethylation reaction (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: LHC demethylation of histone H3K4me2 peptides that contained additional K9ac, K14ac or K18ac showed only minor effects on the demethylation rate, the largest of which was a 60% reduction with H3K4me2K14ac substrate.
source: LHC demethylation of histone H3K4me2 peptides that contained additional K9ac, K14ac or K18ac showed only minor effects on the demethylation rate, the largest of which was a 60% reduction with H3K4me2K14ac substrate (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the presence of SAHA, the demethylase rates of the K9ac and K18ac containing peptide substrates were moderately reduced.
source: The demethylase rates of the K9ac and K18ac containing peptide substrates were moderately reduced while the rate of the K14ac substrate was more sharply inhibited (Figure 3A) with 100 μM peptide substrate.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the presence of SAHA, the rate of the K14ac substrate was more sharply inhibited.
source: The demethylase rates of the K9ac and K18ac containing peptide substrates were moderately reduced while the rate of the K14ac substrate was more sharply inhibited (Figure 3A) with 100 μM peptide substrate.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Deacetylation most likely precedes demethylation in LHC catalysis.
source: These results indicate that deacetylation most likely precedes demethylation, consistent with the more rapid rate of deacetylase activity reported previously (Kalin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citation.

claim: The Km and kcat of LHC demethylase action on the H3K4me2K14ac substrate were dramatically decreased (~20 fold) relative to the non-acetylated substrate.
source: Steady-state kinetic analysis in the presence of SAHA revealed that the Km and kcat of LHC demethylase action on the H3K4me2K14ac substrate were dramatically decreased (~20 fold) relative to the non-acetylated substrate.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: H3K4me2K9ac showed an intermediate effect with ~3 fold reductions in kcat and Km for LHC demethylase action.
source: In comparison, H3K4me2K9ac showed an intermediate effect with ~3 fold reductions in kcat and Km and H3K4me2K18ac was closely matched with the non-acetylated substrate in these LHC demethylase reactions (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: H3K4me2K18ac was closely matched with the non-acetylated substrate in LHC demethylase reactions.
source: In comparison, H3K4me2K9ac showed an intermediate effect with ~3 fold reductions in kcat and Km and H3K4me2K18ac was closely matched with the non-acetylated substrate in these LHC demethylase reactions (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The kcat/Km values were closely matched among the various substrates for LHC demethylase reactions.
source: Interestingly, the kcat/Km values were closely matched among the various substrates suggesting that the reduced catalytic turnover appears to be associated with a stabilized enzyme-substrate ground state complex for H3K4me2K14ac.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The reduced catalytic turnover of H3K4me2K14ac appears to be associated with a stabilized enzyme-substrate ground state complex.
source: Interestingly, the kcat/Km values were closely matched among the various substrates suggesting that the reduced catalytic turnover appears to be associated with a stabilized enzyme-substrate ground state complex for H3K4me2K14ac.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data.

claim: Lys14 acetylation sharply inhibits H3K4me2 demethylation by GST-LSD1.
source: We have specifically investigated Lys9, Lys14, and Lys18 with GST-LSD1 here and found that Lys14 acetylation sharply inhibits H3K4me2 demethylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: LHC preserves an intrinsic property of LSD1 with respect to the H3K14ac inhibitory effects.
source: These results suggest that LHC preserves an intrinsic property of LSD1 with respect to the H3K14ac inhibitory effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of LHC and GST-LSD1 data.

claim: The use of an ester linkage in the synthetic N-tail significantly improved the conversion of H3 from less than 40 to ~90%.
source: In our hands, the use of an ester linkage in the synthetic N-tail significantly improved the conversion of H3 from less than 40 to ~90% (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: LHC was unable to detect nucleosome demethylation even at the highest concentration of LHC employed (400 nM) with 100 nM nucleosome substrate over 3 hr with 146 bp DNA.
source: We investigated the ability of LHC to demethylate H3K4me2 modified nucleosomes by monitoring H3K4me2 disappearance using western blot. However, we were unable to detect nucleosome demethylation even at the highest concentration of LHC employed (400 nM) with 100 nM nucleosome substrate over 3 hr.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: With H3K4me2 mononucleosomes containing 185 bp 601 DNA with 20 bp extensions on either end, LHC catalyzed demethylation was observed, albeit at a slow rate.
source: With this nucleosome with longer DNA, we were able to observe LHC catalyzed demethylation, albeit at a slow rate (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dual LSD1/HDAC1 inhibitor corin could block LHC demethylation activity on 185 bp nucleosomes.
source: To confirm the enzymatic dependence of this demethylation, we showed that the dual LSD1/HDAC1 inhibitor corin (Kalin et al., 2018) could block this demethylation activity. (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rate of LHC demethylation of 185 bp nucleosomes is about 55-fold reduced relative to the corresponding tail peptide substrate.
source: We estimate that the rate of this reaction is about 55-fold reduced relative to the corresponding tail peptide substrate.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data.

claim: LHC showed efficient deacetylation of 100 nM H3K9ac nucleosomes with 20 nM LHC within 20 min.
source: These experiments revealed efficient deacetylation of 100 nM H3K9ac nucleosomes with 20 nM LHC within 20 min with comparatively slower rates measured with H3K18ac followed by H3K14ac (Figure 6A and 7).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: LHC deacetylation of H3K18ac nucleosomes was slower than H3K9ac but faster than H3K14ac.
source: These experiments revealed efficient deacetylation of 100 nM H3K9ac nucleosomes with 20 nM LHC within 20 min with comparatively slower rates measured with H3K18ac followed by H3K14ac (Figure 6A and 7).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Selectivity was preserved with the corresponding triacetylated nucleosomes with K9ac > K18ac > K14 ac.
source: Selectivity was preserved with the corresponding triacetylated nucleosomes with K9ac > K18ac > K14 ac (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a ~7 fold rate differential between H3K9ac and K14ac deacetylation by LHC in nucleosomes.
source: There was a ~7 fold rate differential between H3K9ac and K14ac.
evidence: This is based on comparison of rates in Table 1.

claim: When purified H3 proteins were investigated as LHC substrates, they showed essentially identical rates for hydrolysis at the different positions.
source: Interestingly, when purified H3 proteins were investigated as LHC substrates, they showed essentially identical rates for hydrolysis at the different positions (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The LHC deacetylation rates were much higher for the isolated H3 protein substrates compared with the nucleosome substrates.
source: As observed with LHC catalyzed demethylation, the LHC deacetylation rates were much higher for the isolated H3 protein substrates compared with the nucleosome substrates (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of rates in Table 1.

claim: Both H3K9Hd and H3K14Hd containing nucleosomes could inhibit LHC deacetylase activity with sub-micromolar potencies.
source: We found that both H3K9Hd and H3K14Hd containing nucleosomes could inhibit LHC deacetylase activity with sub-micromolar potencies (Figure 7B) whereas there was little effect of unmodified or acetylated mononuclesomes under these reaction conditions (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Unmodified or acetylated mononucleosomes had little effect on LHC deacetylase activity under these reaction conditions.
source: We found that both H3K9Hd and H3K14Hd containing nucleosomes could inhibit LHC deacetylase activity with sub-micromolar potencies (Figure 7B) whereas there was little effect of unmodified or acetylated mononuclesomes under these reaction conditions (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: H3K14Hd is a competitive inhibitor versus peptide substrate for the LHC reaction.
source: A detailed analysis showed that, as expected, H3K14Hd is a competitive inhibitor versus peptide substrate for the LHC reaction (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on Dixon plot analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The Ki values for H3K9Hd and H3K14Hd containing nucleosomes were 60 nM and 40 nM, respectively for LHC inhibition.
source: The Ki values for H3K9Hd and H3K14Hd containing nucleosomes were 60 nM and 40 nM, respectively for LHC inhibition (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The corresponding H3 Hd-containing proteins and peptides were about 30-fold lower in Ki than nucleosomes.
source: The corresponding H3 Hd-containing proteins and peptides were about 30-fold lower (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The similar potencies of H3K9Hd and H3K14Hd nucleosomes suggest similar accessibility of these nucleosomes for the LHC HDAC1 active site.
source: The similar potencies of these Hd nucleosomes suggest similar accessibility of these nucleosomes for the LHC HDAC1 active site.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar Ki values.

claim: The preference of LHC for deacetylating K9ac versus K14ac in nucleosomes is not a simple difference in exposure but must derive from more subtle interactions such as precise orientation of the acetyl-Lys in the active site.
source: Thus, we deduce that the preference of LHC for deacetylating K9ac versus K14ac in nucleosomes is not a simple difference in exposure but must derive from more subtle interactions such as precise orientation of the acetyl-Lys in the active site.
evidence: This is inferred from the hydroxamic acid inhibition data.

claim: The demethylase and deacetylase activities of LHC are far greater when processing the simpler H3 peptide or protein substrates relative to the nucleosomes.
source: In general, the demethylase and deacetylase activities of LHC are far greater when processing the simpler H3 peptide or protein substrates relative to the nucleosomes, consistent with the idea that the H3 tails are not as sterically available to the LHC active sites in nucleosomes.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The H3 tails are not as sterically available to the LHC active sites in nucleosomes.
source: In general, the demethylase and deacetylase activities of LHC are far greater when processing the simpler H3 peptide or protein substrates relative to the nucleosomes, consistent with the idea that the H3 tails are not as sterically available to the LHC active sites in nucleosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential activity on peptides versus nucleosomes.

claim: The recruitment of LHC by a DNA-binding transcription factor such as REST would significantly enhance LHC targeting to specific regions of chromatin.
source: As the LHC serves a corepressor role in gene regulation, we speculate that the recruitment of LHC by a DNA-binding transcription factor such as REST (Burg et al., 2015; Qureshi et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013) would significantly enhance LHC targeting to specific regions of chromatin.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known biology and supported by citations.

claim: The K14Ac inhibitory effect on LSD1 demethylation is likely through an intramolecular mechanism.
source: We think that the K14Ac inhibitory effect is likely through an intramolecular mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the peptide length requirements and structural data.

claim: The peptide substrate length requirement for efficient processing by isolated LSD1 is a minimum of 20 aa of the H3 tail starting from Ala1.
source: We believe this because the peptide substrate length requirement for efficient processing by isolated LSD1 is a minimum of 20 aa of the H3 tail starting from Ala1 (Culhane and Cole, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: An X-ray crystal structure of LSD1 in complex with an H3 peptide substrate analog shows electron density for the tail peptide extending beyond Lys14 in the complex with LSD1.
source: An X-ray crystal structure of LSD1 in complex with an H3 peptide substrate analog shows electron density for the tail peptide extending beyond Lys14 in the complex with LSD1 (Forneris et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural data.

claim: The vicinity of LSD1 near the Lys14 sidechain is negatively charged.
source: This structure shows that the vicinity of LSD1 near the Lys14 sidechain is negatively charged, and this may account for the reduced activity of the Lys14 acetylation substrate.
evidence: This is based on structural information from cited work.

claim: The negative charge near Lys14 in LSD1 may account for the reduced activity of the Lys14 acetylation substrate.
source: This structure shows that the vicinity of LSD1 near the Lys14 sidechain is negatively charged, and this may account for the reduced activity of the Lys14 acetylation substrate.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural information.

claim: The CoREST complex's gene silencing function will be limited against chromatin marked by H3K14ac.
source: The potential biological implications of this chromatin selectivity are noteworthy since they suggest that the CoREST complex's gene silencing function will be limited against chromatin marked by H3K14ac but more impactful in chromatin lacking this mark.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The CoREST complex will be more impactful in chromatin lacking H3K14ac mark.
source: The potential biological implications of this chromatin selectivity are noteworthy since they suggest that the CoREST complex's gene silencing function will be limited against chromatin marked by H3K14ac but more impactful in chromatin lacking this mark.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Global H3K14ac, relative to H3K9ac, is minimally changed after cells are treated with the HDAC1-3 inhibitor entinostat.
source: However, it is notable that global H3K14ac, relative to H3K9ac, is minimally changed after cells are treated with the HDAC1-3 inhibitor entinostat (Kalin et al., 2018; Schölz et al., 2015), suggesting that the nucleosomal deacetylase selectivity of LHC may be a general property of class I HDAC complexes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The nucleosomal deacetylase selectivity of LHC may be a general property of class I HDAC complexes.
source: However, it is notable that global H3K14ac, relative to H3K9ac, is minimally changed after cells are treated with the HDAC1-3 inhibitor entinostat (Kalin et al., 2018; Schölz et al., 2015), suggesting that the nucleosomal deacetylase selectivity of LHC may be a general property of class I HDAC complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from cellular data cited.

claim: H3K14ac can modulate the structure of the nucleosomal H3 tail as suggested by a computational study.
source: It has been proposed that H3K14ac can modulate the structure of the nucleosomal H3 tail as suggested by a computational study (Ikebe et al., 2016) which could render such nucleosomes resistant to LHC deacetylase action.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a computational study.

claim: The triacetylated H3 tail nucleosomes showed similar deacetylase rates compared with the mono-acetylated nucleosomes.
source: Evidence against this possibility is that the triacetylated H3 tail nucleosomes studied here showed similar deacetylase rates compared with the mono-acetylated nucleosomes.
evidence: This is based on experimental data in Figure 6B and Table 1.

claim: Deacetylation, which is much more rapidly catalyzed than demethylation, is likely to be the first step in dynamic gene silencing by LHC.
source: These studies also clearly show that deacetylation, which is much more rapidly catalyzed than demethylation, is likely to be the first step in dynamic gene silencing by LHC.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative rates of the two activities.

claim: The bi-phasic nature of the LHC demethylase activity suggests that there are at least two different conformations of the LHC complex with altered rate-determining steps associated with the two states.
source: The bi-phasic nature of the LHC demethylase activity remains incompletely understood. We believe it suggests that there are at least two different conformations of the LHC complex with altered rate-determining steps associated with the two states, but more detailed structural studies will be needed to clarify this possibility.
evidence: This is speculation based on the kinetic data.

claim: DNA may be an allosteric activator of LSD1.
source: We hypothesize that DNA may be an allosteric activator of LSD1 and may also play a role as a template to bring substrate and enzyme closer together.
evidence: This is speculation based on the DNA activation data.

claim: DNA may play a role as a template to bring substrate and enzyme closer together.
source: We hypothesize that DNA may be an allosteric activator of LSD1 and may also play a role as a template to bring substrate and enzyme closer together.
evidence: This is speculation based on the DNA activation data.

claim: The hydroxamic acid nucleosomes may prove useful in enhancing structural characterization of a nucleosome-LHC complex by increasing the stability of this association.
source: The hydroxamic acid nucleosomes introduced in this study to probe H3 tail accessibility may also prove useful in enhancing structural characterization of a nucleosome-LHC complex by increasing the stability of this association (Pilotto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation.

claim: The approach of combining F40 sortase and depsipeptide H3 tails offers advantages over native chemical ligation, nonsense suppression, or other methods in combining high yield and efficiency of incorporating tails with multiple and diverse modifications without the need for Cys mutation/desulfurization.
source: We believe that for generating N-terminally modified H3s, this approach offers advantages over native chemical ligation (Holt and Muir, 2015; Seenaiah et al., 2015), nonsense suppression (Neumann et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2017), or other methods (Chalker et al., 2012) in combining high yield and efficiency of incoprorating tails with multiple and diverse modifications without the need for Cys mutation/desulfurization.
evidence: This is based on the improved ligation efficiency demonstrated and comparison with cited methods.

claim: H3K4me2/H3K14ac is a privileged pair of modifications that is especially resistant to CoREST enzymatic processing.
source: We find that H3K4me2/H3K14ac is a privileged pair of modifications that is especially resistant to CoREST enzymatic processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: The CoREST complex is stable for up to 2 weeks when stored at 4˚C at a concentration of about 5 μM.
source: This complex is stable for up to 2 weeks when stored at 4˚C at a concentration of about 5 μM and freeze-thaws were avoided.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations during the study.

claim: LSD1/CoREST can bind to DNA in a DNA sequence independent fashion.
source: It has been reported that LSD1/CoREST can bind to DNA in a DNA sequence independent fashion and that mononucleosomes containing extended DNA sequences are more efficiently demethylated by the LSD1/CoREST heterodimer (Kim et al., 2015; Pilotto et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mononucleosomes containing extended DNA sequences are more efficiently demethylated by the LSD1/CoREST heterodimer.
source: It has been reported that LSD1/CoREST can bind to DNA in a DNA sequence independent fashion and that mononucleosomes containing extended DNA sequences are more efficiently demethylated by the LSD1/CoREST heterodimer (Kim et al., 2015; Pilotto et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and confirmed by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Prior biochemical studies with purified LSD1 have shown that substrate H3 tail acetylation is disruptive to catalysis.
source: Prior biochemical studies with purified LSD1 have shown that substrate H3 tail acetylation is disruptive to catalysis (Forneris et al., 2007; 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The purified LHC complex contains HDAC1, LSD1, and CoREST1 as a heterotrimer in 1:1:1 stoichiometry.
source: We have employed the recently described method to obtain the purified core CoREST ternary protein complex (LHC) which contains HDAC1, LSD1, and CoREST1 as a heterotrimer in 1:1:1 stoichiometry (Figure 2A) (Kalin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is confirmed by the SDS-PAGE in Figure 2A and supported by citation.

claim: InsP6 is an HDAC complex stabilizer.
source: Varying ionic strength, glycerol content, or inositol hexaphosphate (InsP6), an HDAC complex stabilizer (Watson et al., 2016), was performed to see if the kinetic profile could be simplified by adjusting the reaction conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citation.
